title: Hybrid attention and SSM models
summary: Why models like Jamba, Nemotron-H and Qwen3-Next keep a few attention layers among many SSM or linear-attention layers, how the layers are stacked, and what that does to recall and memory.
outcomes: Explain why a fixed-size recurrent state loses exact recall and how a few attention layers restore it
Relate a Mamba-2 layer to gated linear attention through its recurrence and masked-attention dual form
Read the layer pattern of Jamba, Mamba-2-Hybrid, Nemotron-H and Qwen3-Next and state their attention ratios
Compute per-sequence cache memory for a hybrid versus a Transformer at a given context length
Choose an attention ratio and placement from published ablations and name the known failure modes

lessons.title: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not

blocks.md:
Recall from the previous course: a softmax attention layer keeps every past token's key and value in a **KV cache**, so it can look any of them up exactly, but the cache grows with every token. A linear attention or state space model (**SSM**) layer instead folds each token into a **fixed-size state** (a matrix memory), so memory and per-token compute stay constant no matter how long the context gets.

A **hybrid model** stacks both kinds of layers in one network. To see why anyone would bother, we first need to see what the fixed state gives up.

blocks.title: Growing KV cache vs fixed state (toy, 8 tokens)

scenes.caption: After 2 tokens the attention layer has stored 2 separate entries. The SSM layer has 4 state slots, and both tokens are already blended into all of them.
After 4 tokens: 4 cache entries, still 4 state slots. Each slot is now a mixture of tokens 1 to 4.
After 8 tokens the cache has doubled again while the state has not grown. Simplified: real states hold from about 0.1 to 1 million numbers per layer, but they still have a fixed size.

blocks.md: A fixed state behaves like an associative memory with limited capacity. Take the simplest version from linear attention: write each pair with $S \mathrel{+}= v k^\top$ and read with $S k$. With $d$-dimensional random unit keys, every other stored pair adds crosstalk to the read. A short calculation (and the simulation below) gives the expected similarity between what you read and what you stored when $n$ pairs share the state:

blocks.caption: Approximation for random unit keys and values; it agrees with a simulation averaged over thousands of trials (d = 8 and d = 32, n from 1 to 128) to within about 0.02.

blocks.title: Recall quality of a d x d state as pairs pile up

scenes.caption: With d = 8, storing 8 pairs already drops recall similarity to about 0.75, and 64 pairs to 0.33. The cache keeps every pair, so a sharp attention can retrieve it exactly.
Quadrupling the state to d = 32 pushes the curve right (0.58 at 64 pairs) but the shape is the same: any fixed state eventually blurs. Drag d to see it.
Simplified: Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet add decay and smarter writes, which help choose what to keep, but they cannot store an unbounded number of exact pairs in a bounded state.

blocks.prompt: NVIDIA trained 8B-parameter Transformer, Mamba and Mamba-2 models on the same 1.1T tokens and gave them a phone book, then asked for one person's number. The Transformer is near 100% up to its 4096-token training length. Where do the pure SSMs start failing?
blocks.reveal: Far earlier: both start answering incorrectly beyond roughly **500 tokens** of phone book (Waleffe et al., 2024). Their wrong answers share many digits with the right one, which the authors call **fuzzy memory**: the entry was compressed into the state, just not exactly. Training Mamba-2 on 3.5T tokens did not fix it.

blocks.md: AI21's Jamba paper saw the same weakness from another angle. At 1.3B parameters and 250B tokens, a pure Mamba model matched pure attention on perplexity but collapsed on few-shot tasks where the answer must follow the format of the examples. On IMDB it often answered "Very Good" or "3/10" instead of the required "Positive" or "Negative". Adding attention as 1 of every 8 layers fixed it, and the authors found attention heads in the hybrid that point from the final ":" token back to the label tokens of the few-shot examples, like induction heads.

blocks.title: Jamba ablation: pure Mamba fails where copying matters

scenes.caption: IMDB (few-shot sentiment). Pure Mamba scores 48.8 because it ignores the answer format. The hybrid scores 90.9, above pure attention.
QuAC (conversational QA): the hybrid recovers most of the gap (26.6 vs 27.9 for attention, 20.2 for Mamba).
NarrativeQA: 45.8, 27.7 and 43.7. One attention layer in eight is enough to get close to pure attention. All models are 1.3B parameters trained on 250B tokens.

blocks.md: The hybrid bet: SSM or linear-attention layers do most of the sequence mixing cheaply, and a handful of full attention layers act as an exact lookup into the past. The Mamba-2 authors put it as SSM layers being a general sequence-to-sequence map while attention layers are "a retrieval mechanism to quickly refer to previous tokens".

Pure SSMs are not simply worse. In the same NVIDIA study, Mamba-2 trained on 3.5T tokens beat the matching Transformer on average across standard zero-shot tasks. The gap is specific: copying, in-context learning and exact retrieval from the prompt.

blocks.question: A pure SSM answers a phone-book query with 555-284-7710 when the true number is 555-284-7719. What does this suggest?
options: The entry was compressed into the fixed state but cannot be read back exactly
The model never saw the entry, so it guessed a random number
The tokenizer split the digits incorrectly
The model needs positional embeddings to count digits
blocks.explain: Waleffe et al. found SSM answers share many digits with the correct number: information about each entry is in the state, but crosstalk from everything else blurs it. That is the capacity limit of a fixed-size memory, not missing information.

blocks.question: Which task is least likely to separate a pure SSM from a Transformer of the same size and data?
options: Recalling a phone number listed 3,000 tokens earlier
Copying a long string from the prompt
Zero-shot commonsense multiple choice such as PIQA or HellaSwag
Few-shot classification that must reuse exact label strings
blocks.explain: On zero-shot commonsense tasks Mamba and Mamba-2 matched or beat the Transformer in the NVIDIA 8B study. The other three all need exact retrieval or copying from the context, which is where fixed-state models fall behind.

lessons.title: The SSM layer inside a hybrid: Mamba-2 as gated linear attention

blocks.md:
Most recent hybrids (Mamba-2-Hybrid, Nemotron-H) use **Mamba-2** for their SSM layers; Jamba uses the original Mamba. Mamba-2 is easiest to understand as a close cousin of the gated linear attention you already know.

Per head, Mamba-2 keeps a state $h$ of shape (head dim $P$) x (state size $N$). Each token produces an input $x_t$ (like a value), a vector $B_t$ (like a key), a vector $C_t$ (like a query) and a step size $\Delta_t > 0$. The decay $A$ is a single learned negative number per head, so the whole state shrinks by one scalar per step.

blocks.tex: a_t = e^{\Delta_t A}, \qquad h_t = a_t\, h_{t-1} + \Delta_t\, x_t B_t^\top, \qquad y_t = h_t C_t + D\, x_t
blocks.caption: The decode step in the reference implementation (mamba_ssm, Mamba2.step). Compare gated linear attention: S_t = a_t S_{t-1} + v_t k_t^T and o_t = S_t q_t.

blocks.md: The step size is input-dependent, which is what makes the layer **selective**: a large $\Delta_t$ makes $a_t$ close to 0 (forget the past, write the new token strongly), a small $\Delta_t$ keeps $a_t$ near 1 (hold memory). Step through a toy head with $P = 1$, $N = 2$ and $A = -1$.

blocks.title: One Mamba-2 head, 4 tokens, N = 2
blocks.code:
h = [0.0, 0.0]                       # state: N = 2 numbers
for x, dt, B, C in tokens:
    a = exp(-dt)                     # A = -1, so 0 < a < 1
    h = [a*hi + dt*x*bi for hi, bi in zip(h, B)]
    y = sum(ci*hi for ci, hi in zip(C, h))
    print(round(y, 3))

scenes.caption: Token 1: x = 1, dt = 0.5, B = [1, 0]. The write goes to slot 0: h = [0.5, 0]. C = [1, 0] reads slot 0, so y = 0.5.
Token 2: x = 2, dt = 0.5, B = [0, 1]. Slot 0 decays to 0.303 while slot 1 receives 1.0. C = [0, 1] reads it back: y = 1.0.
Token 3: x = 0, dt = 0.1, so a = 0.905: the head mostly holds memory. C = [1, 0] reads slot 0 and gets 0.274, a faded copy of token 1.
Token 4: x = 0 and dt = 3.0 give a = 0.05, which wipes the state. C = [0, 1] reads slot 1 and gets 0.045 instead of about 0.9. One scalar decides how much of everything is kept.

blocks.md: The Mamba-2 paper (Dao and Gu, 2024) shows the same layer can be computed in a second, attention-like way. Unroll the recurrence and the output is a masked attention with no softmax, where queries are $C$, keys are $B$ and the mask multiplies the decays between two positions. This is the **state space duality (SSD)**: a linear-time recurrent form for inference and a quadratic, matmul-friendly form used inside chunks for training.

blocks.tex: Y = \big(L \circ C B^\top\big) X, \qquad L_{ij} = \begin{cases} a_i \, a_{i-1} \cdots a_{j+1} & i \ge j \\ 0 & i < j \end{cases}
blocks.caption: Dual (quadratic) form of SSD, with each row x_j of X already scaled by its step size dt_j (the factor in the recurrence above). With every a_t = 1, L is the plain causal mask and the layer is ordinary causal linear attention.

blocks.title: The decay mask L for 5 tokens

scenes.caption: All a_t = 1: L is the causal mask, so every past token counts fully. This is causal linear attention.
All a_t = 0.9: weight fades geometrically with distance, 0.656 for t0 as seen from t4. Older tokens matter less.
Selective: token t3 has a large step so a_3 = 0.1. Everything before t3 is cut by 10x for all later rows (0.073 for t0 at t4). The model chose to forget.

blocks.md:
For the cache, what matters is the recurrent form. A Mamba-2 layer stores, per sequence, the state $h$ for every head plus a short convolution buffer holding the last few inputs (window 4). In Nemotron-H-8B a layer has 128 heads of dimension 64 and state size 128, so $128 \times 64 \times 128 = 1{,}048{,}576$ numbers, whether the context is 10 tokens or 1 million.

The paper also reports that a dedicated SSD kernel is 2 to 8 times faster than Mamba's fused scan and overtakes FlashAttention-2 from about 2K tokens.

The duality does not make Mamba-2 as good at recall as softmax attention. The quadratic form is a way to compute the same layer faster in training; at inference, all past information still has to pass through the fixed state, and there is no softmax to pick one token sharply.

blocks.question: In a Mamba-2 head, the model sees a token that marks the start of an unrelated document. What setting lets the head discard the old context?
options: A small step size dt, so a stays near 1
A large step size dt, so a falls toward 0
Setting C to zero for that token
Increasing the state size N for that token
blocks.explain: a = exp(dt A) with A negative. A large dt drives a toward 0, which multiplies the whole state by a small number. C only affects what is read, and N is fixed by the architecture.

blocks.question: During decoding at 100K tokens of context, which part of a Mamba-2 layer's per-sequence memory grows with the context?
options: The SSM state h
The convolution buffer
Both, linearly in context length
Neither; both have fixed size
blocks.explain: Both the state (heads x head dim x N) and the convolution window (4 inputs) are fixed by the architecture. That fixed size is exactly why hybrids use these layers, and also why they cannot store unlimited exact detail.

lessons.title: How Jamba, Nemotron-H and Qwen3-Next stack their layers

blocks.md:
A hybrid is defined by its **layer pattern**: which layers mix tokens with attention, which with an SSM, and where the MLPs (or mixture-of-experts layers) go. AI21's **Jamba** (2024), which its authors call the first production-grade attention-SSM hybrid, is the classic example. It repeats a **Jamba block** of $l = 8$ layers with an attention-to-Mamba ratio $a{:}m = 1{:}7$. Each layer is a mixer (attention or Mamba) followed by an MLP, and every $e = 2$ layers that MLP is a **mixture of experts** (MoE) with $n = 16$ experts, of which the top $K = 2$ run per token.

Four such blocks give 32 layers: 52B total parameters, 12B active per token.

scenes.caption: Eight layers in order. Each is a sequence mixer followed by an MLP, with RMSNorm and residual connections (not drawn).
Only layer 4 uses attention, matching the released config (attn_layer_offset 4, period 8). Over 32 layers that is 4 attention layers, so the KV cache is 8x smaller than a same-depth Transformer.
Odd layers swap the MLP for a 16-expert MoE with top-2 routing. This raises total parameters (capacity) while keeping active parameters per token at 12B.
No RoPE anywhere: the paper found results with and without RoPE were similar, presumably because Mamba layers before attention provide position information implicitly.

blocks.md: NVIDIA took a different route. Instead of a repeated block, **Mamba-2-Hybrid 8B** (Waleffe et al., 2024) treats Mamba-2, attention and MLP as separate layers and spreads them evenly: 56 layers = 24 Mamba-2 + 4 attention + 28 MLP, with a Mamba-2 layer first and no position embeddings. **Nemotron-H** (2025) follows the same recipe with extra rules: the first layer is Mamba-2, the last is an FFN, and every attention layer is followed by an FFN. The released Nemotron-H-8B config encodes this as a 52-character pattern string.

blocks.title: Nemotron-H-8B layer pattern (M = Mamba-2, A = attention, F = FFN)

scenes.caption: All 52 layers from the config's hybrid_override_pattern. Mamba-2 and FFN layers alternate; attention appears only 4 times.
The 4 attention layers sit at indices 7, 18, 29 and 40, roughly evenly spaced, and each is followed by an FFN, as in a Transformer block.
24 Mamba-2 layers (46.2%) do most of the token mixing; they hold fixed-size state. 4 of 52 layers (7.7%) are attention, the only ones with a growing KV cache.
24 FFN layers (46.2%) mix nothing across tokens. The 56B model uses the same pattern stretched to 118 layers with 10 attention layers (8.5%).

blocks.md: Hybrids are not limited to Mamba. **Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B** (Alibaba Qwen, 2025) uses the Gated DeltaNet layer from the previous course. Its 48 layers follow the layout 12 x (3 x (Gated DeltaNet then MoE) then 1 x (Gated Attention then MoE)), so one layer in four keeps a KV cache. The attention layers use 16 query heads, 2 KV heads and head dimension 256, and the model card states a native context of 262,144 tokens.

blocks.title: Share of layers that are full attention

scenes.caption: Counting attention layers over all layers that mix tokens or apply an MLP: Jamba 4/32 = 12.5%, Mamba-2-Hybrid 4/56 = 7.1%, Nemotron-H 4/52 = 7.7% and 10/118 = 8.5%.

Counting per mixer instead (attention vs SSM or linear layers, ignoring MLPs) changes Nemotron-H-8B to 4 of 28 = 14.3% and Qwen3-Next stays at 12 of 48 = 25%. Always check which denominator a paper uses.

blocks.md: To read any hybrid's layout, open its config.json: Jamba uses attn_layer_period and attn_layer_offset, Nemotron-H uses hybrid_override_pattern, and Qwen3-Next uses full_attention_interval = 4.

blocks.question: Jamba-v0.1's config has 32 layers, attn_layer_period 8 and attn_layer_offset 4. Which layers (0-based) are attention?
blocks.explain: Attention sits where layer index mod 8 equals 4: layers 4, 12, 20 and 28. The other 28 layers are Mamba, giving the 1:7 ratio.

blocks.question: Why does Nemotron-H place a Mamba-2 layer first and use no RoPE in its attention layers?
options: RoPE is incompatible with grouped-query attention
The first Mamba-2 layer is recurrent and naturally encodes position, so explicit position embeddings are not needed
Attention layers at the start would make the KV cache grow quadratically
Mamba-2 layers require RoPE inputs and must come before attention
blocks.explain: Waleffe et al. put a Mamba layer at the start so the hybrid can work without position embeddings, since the recurrence itself depends on order. Their 840M ablation also found the no-RoPE hybrid did better after long-context extension.

lessons.title: Counting cache bytes: growing KV cache plus a fixed state

blocks.md: The memory win of a hybrid comes almost entirely from the KV cache. For each attention layer, every token stores one key and one value per KV head. Everything below assumes 16-bit (2-byte) numbers.

blocks.tex: \text{KV bytes per token} = 2 \times L_{\text{attn}} \times n_{\text{kv}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times 2
blocks.caption: The first 2 is K and V; the last 2 is bytes per number. L_attn counts only attention layers.

blocks.md: Jamba's paper reports KV cache sizes at 256K tokens (262,144) and the formula reproduces them exactly. Llama-2 7B has 32 layers with 32 KV heads of dimension 128: 512 KiB per token, so 128 GiB at 256K. Mistral 7B and Mixtral use grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads: 128 KiB per token, 32 GiB. Jamba keeps the 8 KV heads but has only 4 attention layers: 16 KiB per token, 4 GiB.

scenes.caption: Full multi-head attention in all 32 layers: 128 GiB, more than a single 80 GB GPU holds.
GQA cuts KV heads from 32 to 8, a 4x saving: 32 GiB for both Mistral and Mixtral.
Replacing 28 of 32 attention layers with Mamba gives another 8x: 4 GiB. The Mamba layers add a fixed state that does not depend on context.

blocks.md:
Now a fair comparison. NVIDIA trained **Nemotron-T-8B**, a 32-layer Transformer, on exactly the same data as Nemotron-H-8B, with the same hidden size 4096 and GQA with 8 KV heads of dimension 128.

- Nemotron-T-8B: $2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131{,}072$ bytes = 128 KiB per token.
- Nemotron-H-8B: 4 attention layers, so 16 KiB per token.
- Plus the fixed Mamba-2 state, computed next.

blocks.caption: Per sequence, from the config: 24 Mamba-2 layers, 128 heads x head dim 64 x state 128, conv channels = inner dim 8192 plus B and C for 8 groups, window 4.

blocks.title: Cache memory per sequence: Nemotron-T-8B vs Nemotron-H-8B

scenes.caption: Below about 456 tokens the hybrid uses more cache memory: its 49.9 MiB of fixed state outweighs the extra KV of the Transformer. Fixed cost, small slope.
At 64K tokens: 8 GiB for the Transformer vs 1.05 GiB for the hybrid, a 7.6x reduction. As context grows the ratio approaches 32/4 = 8x.
Drag a: with 16 attention layers the hybrid's slope is half the Transformer's. The KV saving is set by how few attention layers you keep.

blocks.prompt: Simplified model: after weights, 40 GiB of GPU memory is left for caches. How many 64K-token sequences fit for Nemotron-T-8B, and how many for Nemotron-H-8B?
blocks.reveal: Transformer: 8 GiB each, so **5** sequences. Hybrid: about 1.05 GiB each, so **38** sequences. Larger batches are where much of the throughput gain comes from. Simplified: real servers also need activation memory and allocate cache in blocks.

blocks.md: Compute follows the same shape. When decoding, each attention layer reads all $T$ cached tokens, while a Mamba-2 layer does a fixed amount of work. Waleffe et al. predicted their 8B hybrid would generate tokens nearly 8x faster than the Transformer at long contexts (batch 32). Measured end to end, Nemotron-H-8B was 1.8x and 3x faster than Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B with 65,536 input and 1,024 output tokens on H100s, and Jamba reached 3x Mixtral's throughput at 128K tokens.

Hybrids do not help much at short context. At 1,024 tokens the cache formula gives only about 1.9x less memory for Nemotron-H-8B, and both the Jamba and NVIDIA papers report similar speed to Transformers at small context lengths. The gains grow with context and batch size.

blocks.question: Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B has 12 full attention layers, each with 2 KV heads of dimension 256. How much KV cache does one token need in 16-bit?
options: 6 KiB
12 KiB
192 KiB
24 KiB
blocks.explain: 2 (K and V) x 12 layers x 2 heads x 256 x 2 bytes = 24,576 bytes = 24 KiB. At 262,144 tokens that is 6 GiB, plus the fixed Gated DeltaNet state of the other 36 layers.

blocks.question: An engineer replaces 28 of 32 attention layers with Mamba-2 and is surprised the cache barely shrinks in their chatbot with 300-token conversations. Why?
options: Mamba-2 layers keep a KV cache too
Below the crossover length, the fixed SSM state is as large as or larger than the KV cache it replaced
GQA already removed all KV memory
The KV cache only matters during training
blocks.explain: For Nemotron-H-8B-like sizes the fixed state is about 50 MiB per sequence, as much as about 400 tokens of the Transformer's 128 KiB per token. With the hybrid's own 16 KiB per token added, the two break even at 456 tokens. Short conversations sit below that crossover, so the hybrid's advantage appears only at longer contexts.

lessons.title: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short

blocks.md: How much attention should a hybrid keep? The Mamba-2 paper trained 350M-parameter, 48-layer models on 7B tokens of the Pile, changing only how many of the 48 layers were attention. Everything else, including parameter count and data, was held fixed.

blocks.prompt: Pure Mamba-2 scored perplexity 8.60 and a pure Transformer++ 8.68. If 6 attention layers out of 48 helps, would 24 out of 48 help even more?
blocks.reveal: No. Perplexity is best around 6 attention layers (8.26) and gets worse with more: 24 attention layers give 8.50, close to the pure models. The authors conclude that **around 10%** attention works best. Jamba saw the same flatness: 1:3 and 1:7 ratios scored the same at 1.3B, so AI21 chose the cheaper 1:7.

blocks.title: Perplexity above the best mix (8.26), 350M model, 48 layers

scenes.caption: The two pure models: Mamba-2 is 0.34 above the best hybrid, Transformer++ 0.42 above. Neither layer type alone wins.
A single attention layer removes most of the gap (0.12). By 4 to 6 layers, about 8 to 12% of the stack, the curve is flat at its minimum.
Past that point, more attention hurts: 24 attention layers are 0.24 worse. More attention also means more KV cache, so it loses on both axes.

blocks.md:
Other ablations agree on the main rules:

- **Ratio**: Waleffe et al. found validation loss minimized at roughly 8% attention for 130M models (confirmed at 840M), and that 30% to 50% of layers can be MLPs with no loss increase; 50% MLPs trained 20% faster than 5%.
- **Placement**: spread attention layers out. Mamba-2's authors saw little dependence on exact position as long as attention is not at the very beginning or end; NVIDIA found no pattern better than evenly spaced.
- **Order**: put an SSM layer first so no position embedding is needed.
- **Stability**: Jamba hit large loss spikes at its 7B-based scale from big activations inside Mamba layers, fixed by adding RMSNorm to internal activations.

blocks.title: Four ways to give an SSM model exact recall

scenes.caption: Sequential interleaving: a few full attention layers among many SSM layers. Global exact recall, KV cache in only about 8% to 12% of layers.
Samba (Microsoft) pairs Mamba with sliding window attention of 2048 tokens: constant memory overall, but attention can only see the last window, so exact recall beyond it relies on the Mamba state.

Hymba (NVIDIA) runs attention and SSM heads in parallel inside each layer, then normalizes, rescales and averages them. Only the first, middle and last layers use global attention; the rest use sliding windows.
Qwen3-Next uses Gated DeltaNet instead of Mamba, with one gated attention layer every 4 layers. The recipe is the same: cheap fixed-state mixers plus periodic exact lookup.

blocks.md: Known weak spots from the NVIDIA study: the 16K and 32K hybrids trailed the Transformer by about 1 point on long-context tasks, mostly multi-document QA where distractor passages may confuse the SSM state. Hybrids were also more prompt-sensitive: on Musique the hybrid ranged 10.63 to 16.16 across prompt tweaks vs 15.25 to 17.68 for the Transformer.

Design rule of thumb from published ablations: keep roughly 8% to 12% of layers as global attention, spread them evenly, start with an SSM layer, and expect long-context KV savings close to (attention layers in the Transformer you replace) / (attention layers you keep), at equal KV heads: 32 / 4 = 8x for Nemotron-H-8B vs Nemotron-T-8B, not 52 / 4 = 13x.

blocks.question: A team must cut KV memory but keeps exact recall at 200K tokens. Which design is riskiest?
options: 1 full attention layer per 8 layers, Mamba-2 elsewhere
Mamba layers plus only 2048-token sliding window attention
Gated DeltaNet with a full attention layer every 4 layers
Parallel attention and SSM heads with global attention in the first, middle and last layers
blocks.explain: With only sliding window attention, no layer can look up a token 200K positions back exactly; that recall must survive inside the fixed Mamba state. The other three keep at least a few global attention layers that can read the whole KV cache.

blocks.question: In the Mamba-2 ablation, why is 24 of 48 attention layers worse than 6, beyond just costing more memory?
options: Attention layers cannot be trained with Mamba-2 layers
Too many attention layers cause the SSM state to overflow
Perplexity itself got worse (8.50 vs 8.26) at the same parameter count, so the extra attention displaced more useful SSM layers
The model ran out of position embeddings
blocks.explain: At fixed parameters, every attention layer replaces an SSM layer. The paper measured quality peaking near 10% attention, so going to 50% both raised perplexity and multiplied the KV cache by 4 compared with 6 layers.

blocks.question: Your hybrid is fine on single-document QA but drops on multi-document QA built by packing unrelated passages. What is the most plausible cause based on the NVIDIA study?
options: The attention layers lack RoPE
The SSM layers' state gets confused by irrelevant documents, possibly from training on packed unrelated sequences
The KV cache is too large
The MLP ratio is too high
blocks.explain: Waleffe et al. hypothesized that SSM states are confused by documents irrelevant to the question, and that their long-context recipe of packing unrelated sequences may teach the SSM layers to treat separate documents as related.
